historical_timeline.summary: Born Howard Robard Hughes Jr. in Houston, Texas.
An unexplained paralysis as a boy, after which he developed a lifelong fear for his health.
Critically injured when the XF-11 crashed in Beverly Hills on its first flight; afterwards pain and dependence on codeine.
Flies the large wooden flying boat on its only flight, at Long Beach.
An emotional breakdown; not seen in public afterwards.
Lives on the top floor of the Desert Inn in Las Vegas, then moves between hotels abroad.
Increasing deafness, elaborate procedures against germs, little food and injected drugs.
Dies aboard a plane from Acapulco to Houston; the autopsy finds kidney failure and severe wasting.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Obsessive-compulsive disorder in a wealthy and powerful 41-year-old aviator and businessman with chronic pain after a near-fatal plane crash and long-term codeine use. The episode covers a Y-BOCS severity rating, DSM-5-TR criteria with the insight specifier and the differential (obsessive-compulsive personality, illness anxiety, post-traumatic stress after the crash, psychosis); a structured safety assessment with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; exposure and response prevention as first-line therapy with an SSRI (sertraline, raised to 200 mg) at OCD doses under the APA 1928 guideline and its 1934 watch and NICE CG31, with augmentation options held in reserve; an opioid review under the CDC 1943 guideline with a prescription drug monitoring program check, urine drug testing, naloxone, a nonjudgmental DSM-5-TR assessment that finds opioid use disorder and a switch from codeine to buprenorphine, which treats both the disorder and the pain; non-opioid pain care with physical therapy; audiometry and hearing aids for noise-induced hearing loss; weight, nutrition and kidney function; and how money and household staff can carry out compulsions for a patient and so feed avoidance, with staff involved in treatment only with his consent.

assessment.assessment: The DSM-5-TR criteria are met: intrusive, unwanted contamination obsessions and washing, cleaning and avoidance compulsions aimed at preventing harm, taking more than an hour a day and limiting his work. He recognizes the fears are probably excessive, so the specifier is with good or fair insight; there is no tic history. The rituals are distressing to him, which separates this from obsessive-compulsive personality disorder; his fear is of contamination rather than of having an illness, which separates it from illness anxiety disorder; the PCL-5 of 18 and the absence of re-experiencing argue against post-traumatic stress disorder; and there are no psychotic features. Y-BOCS 28 is in the severe range

An SSRI at OCD doses with exposure and response prevention is first-line under the APA guideline and NICE CG31. Sertraline is preferred to fluvoxamine, which inhibits the enzymes that clear buprenorphine. Start at 50 mg and raise every four to six weeks as tolerated toward 200 mg; OCD often needs higher doses and longer trials than depression, and a fair trial is 8 to 12 weeks with at least four to six weeks at the highest tolerated dose. Check tolerability two weeks after each change and the sodium at follow-up

Exposure and response prevention is the psychological treatment with the best evidence. A hierarchy built with him, from door handles and shared objects to food made by others, restaurants, handshakes and finally the clinic bathroom, with weekly 90-minute sessions and daily home practice, moving to twice weekly once he is engaged. Sessions can be held at the clinic early in the day to protect his privacy

His staff are doing what family members often do: carrying out rituals and giving reassurance, which keeps the fears going. Money and staff remove every natural limit on avoidance. With his written consent, his assistant should join two sessions to learn to step back in planned stages that follow his hierarchy and to offer support instead of reassurance. Staff should not be asked to monitor or report on him

If the Y-BOCS has fallen by less than about 25 to 35 percent after 8 to 12 weeks at the highest tolerated sertraline dose with good exposure therapy, add a low-dose antipsychotic (aripiprazole or risperidone) or switch to clomipramine, with an ECG first. Neither is needed now

Buprenorphine treats the opioid use disorder and helps his pain, and it has no important interaction with sertraline. He has no suicidal ideation; the safety plan, naloxone and weekly dispensing are appropriate. Review suicidal thoughts at each visit, as SSRIs can briefly increase restlessness early on
